items.title: Penalty sets up epic Verstappen charge in his GT return
items.author: Matt Beer
items.content:
Max Verstappen's return to GT racing in the pause between Formula 1 grands prix featured plenty of drama, an eventual top-10 finish, and brought a huge audience (both online and at the track) to the Portimao GT World Challenge event.

A set-up miscue had left the Verstappen team's 2 Seas Motorsport-run Mercedes scraping its way to just 15th on the grid in a shower of sparks during Friday evening's qualifying session.

Verstappen's team-mates Ben Barnicoat and Chris Lulham made rapid progress forward as they took the first two stints, with Barnicoat soon into the top 10 and Lulham charging towards the top five when he took the wheel.

But Lulham then incurred a drivethrough penalty for assisting Luca Stolz's Mercedes into a spin as he tried to take fifth on a restart lap following a safety car.

Lulham took that penalty just before handing over to Verstappen, who therefore took over down in 24th place with just 45 minutes of after-dark racing to go.

Another long safety car cost Verstappen some racing laps to make up ground but did at least close the pack up.

There were 23 minutes left at the restart, with Verstappen 19th by then. He produced a spectacular charge forward that included a particularly entertaining battle with Charles Leclerc's brother Arthur in an AF Corse Ferrari, and managed to at least salvage a top-10 finish in ninth.

That was enough to prompt a massive grin from Verstappen as he got back to the pits, and a huge cheer from the crowd in the main grandstand.

The GetSpeed Mercedes of Ralf Aron, Fabian Schiller and Maxi Gotz took victory.

items.title: Jos Verstappen was hyped like Max - until it all went wrong
items.author: Matt Beer
items.content:
The degree to which Jos Verstappen’s own Formula 1 disappointment fuelled everything he poured into son Max’s preparation for his ultimately-phenomenal F1 career is already part of motorsport folklore.

The element that perhaps gets overlooked now is how good Jos’s own F1 career was supposed to be - that there was a period, a short one admittedly, when there was just as much excitement over Jos’s prospects as a future F1 champion as there was over Max’s arrival on the F1 grid in 2015.

As the latest episode of our new F1 Rewind podcast series with Edd Straw and Mark Hughes explores, it’s a test for Footwork at Estoril in late September 1993 that really starts the hype.

Only two years out of karting, and having just won the German Formula 3 title, 21-year-old Jos sets a time that would’ve put his very middling car 10th on the grid for the previous weekend’s Portuguese Grand Prix. Track evolution played a part in his time, but the impression his overall performance makes is huge. Verstappen gets the cover slot on the next week’s Autosport magazine, which declares him ‘F1’s hottest new boy’.

Edd Straw: “If you look at Jos Verstappen's career record and didn't experience it or live through it, it's really easy to underestimate how big an impact this test really made."

Mark Hughes: “He was a seriously hot property at that time. He came straight in from karting and won championship immediately in GM Lotus in the Benelux Championship. He'd done a one-off guest appearance in the bigger league GM Lotus series at Spa. He was sensational in that.

“He moved straight to Formula 3, won the German championship, dominated it, and looked set to set the F1 tracks alight.

“The teams were falling over themselves trying to get him on a long-term contract. If you were looking for where the next Michael Schumacher or Mika Hakkinen might be, that's where you are looking. No question.”

Edd Straw: “Everybody was talking to him basically. McLaren gave him a test at one stage. Obviously Benetton, who he eventually signed for. There was a little bit of Ferrari interest even. It was an absolute clamour because this was the next mega-star.

“Also because of how rapid his ascent was. Karting to F1 in two years. In recent years we’ve got a bit more used to really fast ascents, such as Max Verstappen’s. But that was really, really rare at this point.

“So you've not only got this driver who is considered to be incredible, but he's on this rocketship to F1 as well.

“And if in late 1993 you were saying, ‘right, who is going to come into F1 and win races and be a future world champion?’ Jos Verstappen is the name people would have picked out.”

Mark Hughes: “Overwhelmingly at that time. There was no question. He was on the verge of something big.”

Verstappen and manager Huub Rothengatter pick Benetton, which is offering a season of testing and preparation in 1994 then a guaranteed race seat - either in its own squad, or placed elsewhere - for 1995.

But rather than getting a year of learning outside the spotlight, Verstappen is thrust into Benetton’s second race seat alongside Michael Schumacher when JJ Lehto is injured in a testing crash.

Verstappen ultimately gets two stints in that seat, with Lehto still struggling on his return and having to step away again, before being benched at the end of the season so Benetton can evaluate Johnny Herbert in that car.

It adds up to 10 of the 16 1994 rounds in the second Benetton, with Verstappen earning two podiums, but also being sent into a terrifying aerial crash on his debut in Brazil in a pile-up triggered by Eddie Irvine and being caught up in the infamous German GP pit fire.

Later admitting he found the Schumacher-centric car “too nervous” for him, Verstappen never outqualified or even once led Schumacher at the end of a racing lap in their eight outings together with a massive 1.920s (2.288%) average deficit.

Going up against Schumacher in the same team as an underprepared rookie, amid a season of turmoil, was a tall order. And it was enough to instantly crush all that career momentum and hype Verstappen had carried into F1.

Mark Hughes: “In hindsight, he wasn't ready, he came in too early. Had the original plan played out, he would have been getting a lot of mileage away from the spotlight of grands prix and would have probably come in much better prepared in 1995.

“Not only that, Benetton was absolutely centred around Michael Schumacher and team boss Flavio Briatore was into driver management and then making money on drivers.

“Rothengatter and Verstappen had unknowingly surrendered control of his own destiny. As well as being in essentially just the second string car in a team that was totally focused around one driver, Verstappen wasn't even going to be in charge of where he was going to go next.”

Edd Straw: “He has this weird season and actually a big chunk of that career momentum's wiped out by that first season. It really, really is. It's not gone. There's still a residual, ‘oh this guy's good’, but already pretty much the die is cast.”

Mark Hughes: “It saps you of energy when you get into a situation like that where you're the second driver and you're not the focus of anything. And you've been used to being at the absolute centre of everything. You've been used to being treated as a megastar in the making and with everything centred around you in the junior category, with everybody there for you, everybody on your side. And suddenly to be in the lackey role, I think it does damage you.

“And not only that, but you're going up against Michael Schumacher as a rookie.

“And in his more reflective later years, Verstappen also said that even disregarding the equipment differences - and there were significant equipment differences at Benetton - and even disregarding all the factors against him, when you looked at some of the things that Michael was able to do close up and suddenly have to say to yourself, ‘I came in thinking I was going to win races, I think I'm going to win the championship, I'm going to beat everybody’ and then you come up against somebody like that and you think, ‘no, maybe I have to recalibrate here’.

“And even Verstappen acknowledges that maybe he wasn't Michael Schumacher.

“But he was pretty good. Better than he was able to show subsequently.”

Watch or listen to F1 Rewind for much more on Jos’s F1 career, including the later big opportunities that fell through, and an in-depth look at how it all fed into the way he handled Max’s upbringing and journey towards F1.

items.title: What one image can't show you about Rwanda F1 track
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
If you adapted the saying 'you should never judge a book by its cover' for the world of Formula 1, then tracks should never be deemed successes or failures based solely on rendered images of them.

What can look like nice lines on a bit of paper are no guarantee that a circuit will be good for racing.

Equally, corners that are spectacular and a thrill for drivers - such as Eau Rouge at Spa, the Degners at Suzuka, or even La Monumental at the newer Madring - look simple affairs when just viewed on a screen.

The disparity between the impression a track render can give and what the reality of a track is like when built is a topic that has come up in recent days following the reveal of the layout of the new F1 track in Rwanda.

The single image released of the new Rise Motordrome track near Kigali, which will host the African Grand Prix from the early 2030s, drew mixed responses from fans - which was perhaps fuelled by some of the key elements of the layout not being visible.

That inevitably prompted debate about whether the track was going to be any good for overtaking.

After years working on the project, and thousands of laps of it on a simulator, track designer Alex Wurz is enthusiastic about what has been pulled together.

And there are so many details to the circuit, which will feature the greatest elevation change over a lap of the season, that are not possible to pick out from the render, according to Wurz.

"To give you a little flavour, in Turn 2, we are coming downhill with top speed," he tells The Race. "It's 10.8% [gradient] exactly. We're going into a very high compression with 12% banking, and then going 14% uphill, so you will only see sky.

"Towards the end of the corner from the 12% banking we are going to 6%, and then 4%. And in the sim, this feels just like pure joy.

"My favourite section is coming out of the canopy corner over the crest into the lake.

"The timing of it is that you just get light [as the car rises over the crest] and then suddenly you get a 10% compression, and from there you know your mind has to engage into the fast Esses.

"Those are the corners I think should resonate with the fans in the simulator, on your computer games, but hopefully with the big dogs - the F1 drivers themselves."

An emphasis on 'fighting'

As a former F1 driver and Le Mans 24 Hours winner, Wurz knows an awful lot about what makes a top-line track, and what ingredients are needed to help make a good race.

He says it is naive to think that overtaking can ever be guaranteed by a track layout because passing is influenced so much by car regulations, details on the day such as tyre degradation levels, and even whether a frontrunner has made a mess of qualifying.

What he thinks is critical though is to produce a track that allows drivers to "fight" each other, and that can only come from how corners are sequenced.

"We have wide open corners with corner sequences 1/2/3, where it means attack, defend, attack, defend," he says. "Now if I defended too much, I might be overtaken, or I'm so slow that the next guy is catching up. So, it is initiating fighting.

"If it finally is the track where the most overtakes are going to happen, to be honest, that's random. It depends which tyre manufacturer, and what tyre degradation on that day will happen.

"But it's a drivers' and riders' circuit. It's made for overtaking and fighting, and I think it should tick all those boxes."

Wurz has faith that what he has designed will not just be good for fighting, but also be a challenge that drivers enjoy.

"I think it will be an amazing circuit for racing, but equally for the drivers," he said. "If people like comparisons, I don't like them too much, but with red wine, you speak about berries and oak flavours.

"So, if we do the same with tracks, you could compare some of the sections to Spa because of the ups and downs and the speed and the flow. Of course, also Suzuka is one of every driver's favourites, and there's some flavours which you could compare.

"But it's all authentic and bespoke to the topography; it's flowing, it's fast, but we do have, of course, heavy braking areas."

One important element that is shared by a lot of tracks is elevation change, something that pretty much all top-ranking venues have.

The 197 metres of elevation that the Rwanda layout boasts should deliver something that will make even the straights spectacular, and was not obvious from the render - which The Race has subsequently produced more of.

The back straight for example, which was actually hidden from the images, plunges downhill before a proper compression as it rises up again into a heavy braking area.

There are also complex braking areas that are being built. "On the render, you don't see the long straight well, and you don't see the hairpins," says Wurz.

Effort has gone into creating tight turns with combined braking/turning where drivers are exposed to greater risks of getting things wrong - and therefore being attacked from behind.

"What is really challenging is if you are combining forces: your braking, your turning, to then optimise all four contact patches at the right slip angle," says Wurz.

"So those corners where you arrive at 300km/h and you break down to something like 80km/h or 100km/h, but with long combined phases, they are the ones where you can do the real divebombs. And we have three of those.

"I think those will be the sneaky overtakes. And if you start to defend, again, then your next straight line will be three and a half to four tenths down. And that triggers the fighting.

"And if there is no overtaking from that, triggering the fighting means someone else is coming. So I think it should at least initiate great fighting."

Wurz has consulted a lot of driver friends with ideas for the layout, and says that feedback has been positive.

While he has not identified those he has consulted, he says that drivers with a total of 12 FIA world championships have been involved. As chairman of the Grand Prix Drivers' Association, the likelihood is that some of those titles were from F1.

Wurz thinks that, in order to make a layout a good drivers' circuit, it is critical that drivers have input on what works.

"I am in almost everyday contact with the greatest champions of current times, so I do show them tracks," he says. "I do listen to what is said about corner sections and which are rewarding and not rewarding.

"They always have some tips, but the principle layout was seen by one guy who texted me back he said: 'That will be instantly one of the most classic favourite circuits of all drivers.' And I really hope so because it is a lot of work!"

And if you want a hint of the way that the track layout has been shaped by thinking about the challenge drivers face, then there is no better example than the Esses section at the end of the lap.

Wurz says this area, which looks similar to but is not a carbon copy of the Suzuka Esses, is one that is going to punish greedy drivers who try to attack it too much.

"If you get one element wrong, the next five or six corners are off," he says. "That's havoc in your brain, but it's joy if you manage it.

"You are coming around the lake out of the forest corner, which is a really cool corner because it's only forest and the track, and then you come over a hill into a double right-hander.

"Here the lift in the stomach should be perfectly timed to then get the compression on the apex. And from this moment on, every movement you do on your instruments are important: steering, throttle and brake.

"None of the corners are flat. Everything has to be either just a downshift or dab on the brake. You really need to flow from one to the next.

"If you do a little mistake, it's designed that greed is penalising you. And this is so cool for the drivers because you kind of have to hold back a little bit, but you want to exceed it.

"If you slide half a metre too wide, that means you have already 0.15 seconds gone, so you have to be true to yourself. And this is a type of mind game.

"Suzuka does it very well. That's why all the drivers love it, and hopefully we can be in the same category of racetrack as the great ones."

items.title: Verstappen has troubled qualifying in latest GT outing
items.author: Matt Beer
items.content:
Max Verstappen and team-mate Chris Lulham and Ben Barnicoat will start only 15th for the GT World Challenge race at Portimao that Verstappen is contesting in his break between Formula 1 races.

Verstappen's return to the GT scene got off to an eventful start as he tapped Ezequiel Perez Companc's Audi into a spin in a traffic jam on his first lap in morning practice.

Stewards looked at the incident but took no action, and by the end of the second practice session the Verstappen crew was up to fourth.

But they struggled in qualifying, their Mercedes visibly running lower than most and kicking up abundant sparks in the twilight session as they managed only 15th on the 61-car grid.

While Barnicoat called 15th a "could be worse" situation, he admitted the 2 Seas Motorsport-run Verstappen team had taken a wrong turn with the set-up.

"We felt like we'd been missing a little bit of speed - we've been quite high up the timesheets but none of us were super happy," he said.

"So we tried a couple of things there and obviously it didn't quite work out - lots of sparking, a lot of bouncing in a straight line, so I think we just missed it a little bit."

The three-hour race starts at 5pm local time on Saturday. The Boutsen VDS Porsche of Dorian Boccalacci, Morris Schuring and Alessio Picariello starts from pole.

items.title: How Horner, Brown and Wolff made their fortunes from F1
items.author: Darren Cox
items.content:
Christian Horner, Zak Brown and Toto Wolff have been three of the most influential team bosses during Formula 1's extraordinary growth over the past decade.

All three have been very well rewarded for it. But the latest set of F1 team accounts filed in the UK reveal something more interesting than simply how much each has made.

They show three very different ways of sharing in the value that has been created as F1 teams have gone from businesses that often needed wealthy owners to keep funding them to scarce sporting assets now worth billions.

Horner was ultimately a very highly paid employee at Red Bull. Brown has participated in McLaren's growth through a long-term incentive scheme. Wolff owns a significant part of the Mercedes team he runs.

The difference between the three helps explain why ownership now appears to be so important to Horner as he considers what he does next.

Red Bull Technology's 2025 accounts disclose £66.988million in compensation for loss of office for its highest-paid director, understood to be Horner, alongside £9.029m in remuneration.

That puts his disclosed package for the year at around £76m.

Some reports have put the compensation above £100m by adding a separate £33.494m figure contained in Red Bull Racing's accounts. But Red Bull Technology explicitly states that its £66.988m disclosure is for the group, which includes Red Bull Racing. The £33.494m should therefore not be added again.

Even £76m is an extraordinary sum.

But perhaps the most interesting thing about Horner's 20 years at Red Bull isn't what he made. It's what he didn't have: ownership.

That should not be confused with Horner having made a bad deal when he joined Red Bull. Quite the opposite.

At the end of 2004 he was 31, had built a successful Formula 3000 team in Arden, and was trying to find a way into F1. He had looked at buying Jordan but simply didn't have the hundreds of millions required to make the step independently.

Then Dietrich Mateschitz bought Jaguar and turned it into Red Bull Racing.

Horner later recalled being summoned to Salzburg and Mateschitz telling him he had big ambitions for the team and was "willing to take a chance" on him. Horner said he was only 31 and "didn't have to think about it for too long".

And the deal itself wasn't bad either. Horner has since recalled that Mateschitz told him he wouldn't be paid a huge salary but would receive a healthy bonus for every point Red Bull scored. Jaguar had managed nine points the previous season. Red Bull scored 34 in its first.

For a 31-year-old team owner trying to find his way into F1, it was an extraordinary opportunity.

Horner helped turn Red Bull Racing from the remains of Jaguar into one of F1's most successful teams, winning six constructors' championships and eight drivers' titles.

But however well he was rewarded, Horner remained an employee of a business owned by somebody else.

Brown's situation at McLaren is different.

McLaren Racing's accounts show its highest-paid director received £81.897m in 2025, comprising £8.215m in remuneration and £73.682m relating to its long-term incentive scheme. Brown has been identified as that director in reporting of the accounts.

The bulk of the package resulted from an incentive scheme connected to the enormous increase in the value of McLaren Racing.

The turnaround has been remarkable. McLaren was in serious financial trouble during the pandemic and brought outside investment into its racing operation. Five years later, the transaction that consolidated the ownership of McLaren Racing valued the business at around £3.5billion.

Brown therefore had a substantial participation in the increase in McLaren Racing's value through his incentive arrangements, allowing him to share in the upside as the business was transformed.

The comparison with Horner is striking. Both received packages of around £80m in 2025, but they got there in completely different ways.

Horner's was dominated by the compensation he received for leaving the business he had spent two decades building. Brown's was dominated by an incentive designed to give him a share of the value created as McLaren Racing grew.

Wolff's position is different again. Mercedes' accounts disclose £9.528m of total directors' remuneration in 2025, although they don't tell us how much of that was Wolff's individually.

His executive pay is, in any case, almost incidental to the important number. Because Wolff owns the asset.

When INEOS bought into Mercedes' F1 operation, the team was divided equally between Mercedes-Benz, INEOS and Wolff's investment vehicle. Wolff therefore had a one-third economic interest in Mercedes F1 while also serving as its team principal and CEO.

That also allows him to participate in the profits distributed by the business. Mercedes paid £125m in dividends in 2025, meaning a one-third shareholder would have an economic interest in roughly £42m of that if the distribution was made pro rata. That money would, of course, flow through the relevant ownership structures rather than simply appearing as part of Wolff's salary.

But last year provided a much bigger indication of what his original investment has become worth.

Mercedes confirmed the structure but did not disclose the price. The transaction was reported as valuing Mercedes F1 at around $6bn, with Wolff receiving approximately $300m for the stake he sold.

And he only sold 15% of his holding.

Wolff retained the remaining 85%, equivalent to approximately 28.3% of Mercedes F1. At the same $6bn valuation, that stake would be worth around $1.7bn.

That isn't $1.7bn sitting in Wolff's bank account. It is the implied value of a shareholding based on the valuation attached to a minority transaction.

But it shows the enormous difference between being paid to create value and owning the value you create.

Horner spent more than two decades building Red Bull Racing and was extremely well rewarded as an employee, including a remarkable payment when that relationship ended.

Brown helped take McLaren Racing from the edge of a financial crisis to a business valued at around £3.5bn, with an incentive structure that allowed him to participate directly in that increase in value.

Wolff did something different. He bought into the business he was running.

As the value of F1 teams has exploded, that has proved to be the ultimate deal.

Which brings us back to Horner.

Since leaving Red Bull, he has become increasingly clear about wanting something different from the next stage of his career.

His language now is particularly interesting when compared with the 31-year-old who described the original Red Bull opportunity as a "no-brainer".

"I've been a hired hand," Horner said recently. "I did 21 years sitting on the pitwall. I don't need to go back to that."

His preference now is to return as "a partner, rather than just a hired hand".

It isn't difficult to understand why.

The original Red Bull deal was a fantastic one for Horner in 2005. What changed over the following 21 years was F1 itself, and particularly the value of its teams.

F1 teams were once sporting operations that routinely consumed their owners' money. Today, the best of them are global sports businesses worth billions.

If Horner is going to spend the next decade helping to build another one, you can see why this time he appears determined to own a piece of it.

items.title: Lawson launches custom guitar ahead of the US GP
items.author: Hannah Atkinson
items.content:
F1 driver by day, musician by… Thursday evening? Liam Lawson will make his debut in VCARB's Garage Sessions music and culture event ahead of the United States Grand Prix at Austin, while launching his very own custom Taylor Guitars LL30 GS Mini Special Edition. 

The guitar features a pink to white ombre design, and his racing number 30 in the centre.

Liam has loved music since his childhood, as his Dad encouraged him and his brother to play from the age of six. Not quite the career path Liam ended up taking, though.

The event kicks off on Thursday at Inn Cahoots on Austin’s East 6th Street, with the Esses Bazaar from 3pm, featuring live music, food, western wear, glam stations, tattoos and a chance to get up close and grab a photo with the team’s show car.

Garage Sessions follows at 7pm, where Liam will perform live next to his former childhood bandmates, including his brother and two close friends!

The wider line up features a mix of emerging talent and established songwriters like Jonathan Capeci, Scoot Teasley, Jess Farren, Alison Nichols, and Drake Milligan.

Liam said: “I feel very proud to be launching my partnership with Taylor Guitars at Garage Sessions. Playing the guitar has been a big part of my life since I was young, as my Dad played in a band throughout my childhood. He encouraged my brother and I to play since we were six years old, so it feels like a full circle moment to be launching a custom LL30 GS Mini SE while performing with my brother and two friends who I grew up playing with.

"Music is a big part of my life, and I use it to clear my head during the season, so I'm really excited to perform at Garage Sessions where we can connect with fans outside of the track. I’m look ing forward to meeting everyone there.”

With Garage Sessions bringing together racing, music, and community, Racing Bulls is giving fans another reason to get excited about Austin, and giving Lawson a chance to show off a skill that doesn’t involve a steering wheel.

items.title: The extraordinary figures hinting at Aston Martin's pole potential
items.author: Mark Hughes
items.content:
As the strains on the relationship between Aston Martin and its Formula 1 power unit partner Honda continue and speculation inevitably questions the future of the partnership, it's a good time to look at how the AMR26-Honda is actually performing beyond just the headline depressing Q1 ejections.

While Sepang - where both cars made it through to Q2 for the first time - offered a ray of hope, it was dashed one week later in Singapore where Alonso felt certain the power unit's turbo must be broken, so poor was its performance. Honda later reported it could see no failure...

It begs the question of just where would this car be if it had a competitive power unit? Is it a mediocre car, a rare Adrian Newey dud, with a poor engine? Or a good car with a truly terrible engine?

If we look at the car's performance through the season in the accompanying graph, two things are very clear. 1) The step-change worsening of the car's competitiveness from Barcelona (round seven) to Spa (round 10) as the top teams piled on their developments while the AMR26 remained still in race one spec. 2) The step-change improvement from the car's sole update, in Hungary (round 11). But where does that updated car truly stack up in the quality of its chassis?

We can break down the performances further by looking at GPS data from each track and assessing how much time the car loses in those sections of track taken at full throttle (ie mainly the straights). It's an inexact science because of the confounding number of skewing factors* but it does give an order of magnitude picture which is quite clear.

The following is quite a reductive stat but a significant one. Comparing Max Verstappen's pole time at Sepang to Fernando Alonso's 12th-fastest time, the Aston Martin driver is 2.090s behind despite having surrendered 2.238s to the Red Bull on the full-throttle parts of the lap. The inference is that with power parity Alonso could've been on pole by a tenth and a half.

What is even more eye-opening is that despite the huge disappointment of Singapore, where Alonso went out in Q1 convinced the turbo was broken, the car's corner performance was even more competitive than at Sepang.

It's never quite that simple and we'd need to know comparable drag and downforce numbers throughout the compared speed range too, obviously not something the teams are going to release - to each other or to us. But since that Hungary upgrade, Alonso has been driving a car with a balance and poise that he has praised.

But the hoped-for follow-up of a power unit improvement from Honda has not manifested. While Alonso's praise of the car on the cooling lap at Zandvoort after getting ninth-place points - "Thanks to everyone at Silverstone. Amazing. A lovely car to drive." - coincided with the introduction of the ADUO 1 Honda upgrade, the feedback from both drivers was that it had lost the driveability gains which had been made with the previous version.

When we do the comparison of the Aston Martin to the pole car at each of the tracks since it got its Hungary aero upgrade, we get the following:

Laptime deficit when not on full throttle

: +1.310s (actual: 2.601s; on full throttle: 1.291s): 1.011s (actual: 2.487s; on full throttle: 1.476s): 0.237s (actual: 3.364s; on full throttle: 3.127s): 1.003s (actual: 3.564s; on full throttle: 2.561s): 2.203s (actual: 4.057s; on full throttle: 1.854s): -0.148s (actual: 2.090s; on full throttle: 2.238s): -0.370s (actual: 2.85s; on full throttle: 3.22s)

We can derive a further set of stats from those numbers, that of an implied percentage split of the deficit between power unit-limited and chassis-limited sections of the lap for each of those tracks.

: 49.6% / 50.4%: 59.3% / 40.7%: 92.9% / 7.1%: 52% / 48%: 47% / 53%: 101% / -1%: 113% / -13%

These numbers suggest the car, even after its Hungary upgrade, was losing time in the corner and the full-throttle sections, but with the power unit forming the dominant part of the deficit, varying wildly according to track layout. But at Sepang and Singapore it was faster through the corners than the pole car.

Although factually correct we should treat the above numbers with caution (read the small print*). But they do describe a basic outline, one in which corner performance is more than respectable, recently even very impressive.

Worryingly though, as the chassis performance has steadily improved, the power unit appears to be worse with each ADUO upgrade.

The ADUO 1 unit came one race after Hungary, at Zandvoort, and the deficit at full throttle increased by a couple of tenths. This may be nothing more than the respective track layouts but, as recalled, the driver feedback suggested little or no overall progress from the power unit there.

Attending to those driveability issues via a turbo modification resulted in the ADUO 2 spec, which Alonso first got in Baku. This was the power unit in the car when it had such an encouraging run at Sepang, but the intricate corner-upon-corner layout of Singapore triggered it into a nightmare of terrible throttle response and wildly inconsistent deployment.

If the AMR26 could magically be given power unit parity, would it really have been fighting for pole? Not until Sepang, no. Until then, the numbers suggest that since its Hungary upgrade it would have been a high Q2/lower Q3 car. But from Sepang, quite possibly yes. Even in Singapore.

But again, there is a disclaimer about that. For it is quite possible that the Honda power unit's unique architecture (with the MGU-K up front, as requested by Newey, centralising the car's mass) has flattered the car's cornering performance. And that with a more powerful, conventionally configured Mercedes or Red Bull power unit, it could possibly lose that cornering advantage.

But while taking on board the many cautious disclaimers, we can get an order-of-magnitude idea of the split between chassis and power unit responsible for the big laptime deficit of the Aston Martin. A much more detailed version of that picture will be at the very heart of ongoing discussions between the team and Honda and about what the future might hold for the partnership.

*: Some of the deficit of the Aston Martin to pole will be track evolution between whatever session the Aston Martin goes out in compared to Q3. That track evolution will vary from event to event.

If we compared the Aston Martin times to the fastest of the session in which Aston Martin was eliminated it would be equally misleading as the quick cars are typically just doing enough to comfortably get through while saving tyres and full power for Q3 while the slow cars are flat-out.

The chosen downforce levels will also skew the chassis vs power unit picture (ie low wing would make the power unit look better than it is).

items.title: Why one F1 test day decided a 2027 driver choice
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Haas would have likely made a different choice for its 2027 Formula 1 driver line-up if it hadn't started its own Testing of Previous Cars programme last year.

He became the "crystal clear" choice with his strong performance in an old-school 'F1 shootout' at Portimao, as part of that TPC run in a 2025 Haas, having fended off that competition.

Asked if the logic for signing Camara went beyond him being the fastest driver in the Portimao test day, Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu simply said: "He was the quickest. That was a very simple answer. Definitely, yeah. He was impressive."

Camara's Portimao competition included McLaren's Formula 2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli and Ryo Hirakawa, the top F1 prospect of one of Haas's key backers, Toyota - which was instrumental in Haas having a TPC programme in the first place.

Together with Toyota, Haas's TPC programme had already given test opportunities to ex-F1 drivers Kamui Kobayashi, Kazuki Nakajima, Romain Grosjean and Super Formula champions Sho Tsuboi and Ritomo Miyata over the first year and a half of the project.

But the biggest vindication of the TPC project so far came in August, with the Portimao shootout test being vital to Haas's 2027 driver choice.

"This is part of the reason why we wanted to have a capability to do a TPC [programme]," Komatsu said.

"Then last year was about getting off the ground, operating professionally, creating a good culture, a good team.

"Then this year we knew that we have to be able to evaluate drivers. We can anticipate that because of the contractual situation of our drivers [Ocon and Ollie Bearman's contracts expire at the end of 2026].

"We had the capability, therefore we could assess it by ourselves. But without doing that one, I cannot be nowhere near as confident, right?

"Then I don't know if I made the same decision, seriously. I don't, probably not. I don't know because Formula 2 from outside is very, very difficult to understand.

"All you guys were questioning when I took Ollie for a '25 seat, 'Ollie's not performing in F2 [he finished 12th in 2024]. Are you sure that's the right choice?' I had a question from many of you, but I was confident because we had access to Ollie through FP1s. I knew what he was capable of.

"We knew what he was capable of and what kind of personality he is etc. So without doing this TPC, if we decided to take Rafa without doing it, it certainly feels much more like a gamble.

"Then do I want to gamble like that? Probably not, but it's a hypothetical situation. This is why we put the environment in place so that we can take it under our control."

'Equally exciting' potential to Bearman

Just three days separate Bearman and Camara in age, and both will have spent five years on the junior ladder before graduating full-time to F1.

Both demonstrated devastating raw pace below F1 despite some rough edges - Camara is leading the F2 championship, but there have been lost wins and podiums through incidents.

So The Race asked Komatsu if he feels there are some parallels between the two: "Yeah, in terms of potential we see, I would say equally exciting. Very, very similar.

"But in the details, I think it's different because what impressed me most with Ollie was how he understood the overall situation, how he understood his role, how he executed in FP1 in Mexico [2023], first time in F1 car.

"That's a very different scenario to what Rafa had in Portimao, which was a clear, clear shootout, right? The first time he's jumping in our car. So speed, honestly, excitement about the speed, I would say similar.

"But in terms of how we were impressed with Rafa, it's really that judging those conditions, because you got to have a very, very good feel for the car about the grip, to be able to judge those ever-so-changing conditions.

"The condition was changing every minute, every lap, right? No two laps are the same. So that was impressive. But also knowing it's a shootout, how he, let's say, created his environment so that he could focus on what he needs to do and how he wasn't fixated on the outcome.

"He focused on what he needed to do to be himself, to get his best performance, to then understand what the mechanism for him to do that and then execute was very impressive.

"Other than the speed, it's like 'wow' - it's just potential how we can grow together, how we can nurture this talent, how we can flourish, is a potential. So that is the common, exciting factor."

Bearman hasn't been officially confirmed as Camara's 2027 team-mate but it appears to be a matter of time.

"I'd like to continue with Ollie, he's an incredible talent and he showed amazing growth," Komatsu said.

"Then this year, he's shown that he's ready to be a team leader. Also, how he raced in Singapore [he charged from 13th to sixth in the sprint], which was very, very impressive.

"It's just a matter of timing [and] finalising certain details. But yes, it is our intention to continue with Ollie, but then a formal announcement will come in due course."

What of the other candidates?

Ocon has ruled himself out racing in another series in 2027 and is likely to take a reserve driver role elsewhere on the grid next year.

Komatsu spoke highly of the three drivers Camara beat in the shootout. "The good thing of all those driver selection processes was all drivers who were involved in that did a very, very good job. Rafa, Leo Fornaroli, Ryo Hirakawa, Jack Doohan. I believe they all got the best out of themselves and every time they got in the car, they improved.

"So that was honestly a very, very uplifting process to be involved with."

Asked specifically about Haas’s reserve driver Doohan continuing with the team into 2027, Komatsu said: "Our door's open, definitely. We've been talking with him and then his manager as well to see if we can do something together beyond this year.

"So that's still an open question."

And given Toyota was so instrumental to Haas's TPC programme, providing both finance and engineers for it, how did it feel about Haas picking a Ferrari-backed driver over one of its own in Le Mans 24 Hours winner Hirakawa?

"From the very moment we started talking with Toyota in 2024, I knew that Akio-san [Akio Toyoda, Toyota chairman] was very keen to get one of his drivers to the race seat next year, 2027," said Komatsu.

"So I went to see him in person, in Tokyo, before we signed anything, before he made any comment, because I didn't want any misunderstanding. I didn't want him to, let's say, invest in the team with a misunderstanding of, 'OK, if we work together, we can get one of my drivers to the race seat'.

"I said to him, 'Look, I understand your target, but this driver, whoever your driver is going to be, has to be the fastest one, because if I chose the driver who is not the fastest, who is not the best, they're going to be labelled as, OK, Toyota just poured the cash in to get their driver into F1'.

"Then whoever this driver is who got the seat, because of Toyota backing, is going to be labelled as a 'Toyota pay driver'. Then we're not going to produce the result that we should be producing, because this guy's not the fastest guy.

"So, for all three parties involved, it's not going to work, is it? So, I was totally transparent from the start: 'Akio-san, we're going to choose the driver who is the fastest'. And then he's completely happy with that.

"Initially, when we told him the plan to assess Ryo Hirakawa alongside some other drivers, he was actually very happy to say, 'Wow, Haas is doing it properly in this way'.

"That shows the calibre of the person, I think. He was never expecting his driver, in this case, Ryo Hirakawa, to be given a seat without merit, right? And then he was assured that we are doing it as professional and as fair way as possible that we can execute.

"Once I made a decision, and then I went to see him on Monday after Singapore, because we had another event, but that was a good chance for me to catch up with him.

"So, I told him in person with everything, all the process etc which he knew anyway. It was important for me to, again, look at his eyes in person to just tell him. He was absolutely fine. But he's that kind of person. He's great.

"So, I cannot be grateful enough that we have this collaboration that I actually met him."

items.title: Williams to stage London display for 50th anniversary celebrations
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
The Williams Formula 1 team will mark its 50th anniversary with what it calls "year-long celebrations" of its heritage, headlined by a commemorative display in London.

Six cars that represent significant moments in both Williams and F1 history will be part of the team's 'W50 Live' display at 26 Leake Street in central London, off Waterloo's iconic under-station graffiti tunnel, alongside an F1 showcar complete with the team's 2027 livery.

The car that uses that livery in competition will be known as the FW50, Williams has officially announced.

That is in keeping with its famous FW chassis moniker, in honour of founder Frank Williams, as the team 'skips' the FW49 name to mark the 50th anniversary of the F1 team's first race in 1977, when it ran as Williams Grand Prix Engineering.

The Leake Street display - which runs from February 11-28 and will be open to the public as a ticketed event - will include the first F1 car produced by Williams Grand Prix Engineering, the FW06, as well as the FW11B, FW14B, and FW19 cars driven to world championship success by Nelson Piquet in 1987, Nigel Mansell in 1992, and Jacques Villeneuve in 1997 respectively.

Williams has chosen to also note two F1 milestones with its other two car choices: the 2003 FW25 set the record for the fastest average speed in F1 history through Juan Pablo Montoya, which stood for 17 years, while 2016's FW38 still has the record for the highest speed ever reached by an F1 car, when Valtteri Bottas hit 378km/h (234.9mph) during that year's Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend.

It will also give fans the chance to choose the livery for its home race, the British GP at Silverstone. This is believed to be a full branding takeover including Alex Albon and Carlos Sainz's racesuits, team kit and garage as well as the car.

Limited-edition merchandise to honour "some of the standout moments, personalities and car designs that have made Williams what it is today" will be produced, including a W50 Monopoly set that is due to go on sale before Christmas.

Williams has promised there are "many more 50th anniversary moments to be revealed over the coming months".

Tickets for the 'W50 Live' event will go on pre-sale later this month. Members of Williams's W Club will have access to this on October 26, before a general sale follows on October 29. More information can be found at williamsf1.com/w50live

items.title: Our verdict on Haas signing Camara for F1 2027
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Is that a good move? What can we expect from Camara, and what does it mean for his 2027 team-mate Ollie Bearman?

Here's what our team thinks:

A fantastic wildcard addition to F1's 2027 grid

If Rafael Camara is as exciting as I've been told he looked in his Haas F1 test debut, then he is a fantastic wildcard addition to the F1 grid. 

His credentials from his junior career make him a worthy graduate anyway. This is a driver who was among the best in karting, and has now pieced together a rare run of consecutive titles higher and higher up the single-seater ladder. 

Winning championships is never easy but that alone isn't a guarantee of the kind of ability or traits that will then thrive in F1. The work done in F1 machinery, even in brief opportunities, often counts for far more. 

Haas was obviously aware Camara was a promising prospect from his feeder series CV. But, I'm told, it was won over comprehensively when Camara drove its car at Portimao. He was so fast that some in Haas believe that Ollie Bearman - who drove briefly on the day to establish a reference - wouldn't have been as quick even with a proper runplan. 

That's not to say Camara is faster or a better prospect than Bearman. But he's that level: rapid, and with an instantly good impression. So it will be fascinating to see if this translates. 

Where he's a gamble most is his racecraft and decision-making, which is unpolished based on his Formula 2 error rate - although, ironically, that's something that went for Bearman in his rookie season last year too...

This is the next proper test of Bearman's credentials as a potential future Ferrari F1 driver.

It's almost seemed pre-ordained since he burst onto the scene in Saudi Arabia as the stand-in for Carlos Sainz while Sainz had his appendix removed.

The performances Bearman put up against Nico Hulkenberg, while Kevin Magnussen was suspended and then unwell, only strengthened the feeling Bearman is something special and would eventually replace Lewis Hamilton at the Scuderia.

Bearman has seen off Esteban Ocon fairly comfortably, in terms of raw speed at least. I do think Ocon's greater experience has helped the team, but Ocon isn't overall fast enough, consistently enough, versus Bearman to justify what Haas was paying him, as well as the spiky attitude Ocon apparently had behind the scenes within that team.

Camara brings a new dimension - another highly-rated F2 graduate, with similar Ferrari Academy support that propelled Bearman to F1, and there's the added dynamic of Camara's impressive Testing of Previous Cars performance at Portimao.

Camara hasn't gone properly head-to-head with Bearman yet, but there's no doubt in my mind that (commercial considerations aside) Haas feels it now has a driver on its books that it expects to give Bearman a properly hard time.

If the hype isn't real, then Bearman has nothing to fear, but if Camara is as good as he appears to be from what we've heard so far then Bearman is going to need to find another gear in 2027.

His mission is to stop Camara from becoming the new flavour of the month, ultimately trying to make sure the next new kid on the block doesn't reach Ferrari before he does.

The ideal driver line-up for Haas

This feels like the ideal driver line-up vibe for a team in Haas's position - a well-established underdog that can score semi-regularly if its drivers maximise their chances and fortune falls its way.

Two drivers trying to climb over each other to prove themselves to F1's most legendary team, which also happens to be the top squad most likely to have a vacancy in the medium-term future given Hamilton's career position. There's everything to fight for and zero risk of complacency.

Plus, Bearman is now relatively experienced enough to lean on as a quasi-leader/benchmark.

Last time Haas went all in on youth for its driver line-up, it was obviously a terrible experience, but a cash-strapped holding pattern year with an undeveloped car driven by Mick Schumacher and Nikita Mazepin was a very different prospect to what Haas has got in store for 2027 with Bearman and Camara.

The fact that it held a proper old-school shootout for the seat with such a varied line-up of candidates makes it an even better story. 

Camara has F1's most important trait

Camara getting a shot at F1 is richly deserved, and it's the kind of anti-conservatism driver choice that rival teams should take note of.

He's had a fascinating junior career so far, starting off in the (huge) shadow of Kimi Antonelli in Formula 4 and the Formula Regional European Championship.

But Camara didn't panic. He took the slow path, staying in FREC another year, growing as a driver and dominating that season before adding the Formula 3 crown one year later, while Antonelli made his F1 debut.

He arrived in F2 and demonstrated arguably the best raw pace in the category since Charles Leclerc.

There have been rough edges. He's not had the same devastating execution as the likes of Leclerc. But he shares the trait all successful F2-F1 graduates have had: sheer raw pace.

It's that speed that's prompted Haas to take a gamble on him, and it will be that speed that will go a long way to helping Camara establish himself in F1.

items.title: Ferrari F1 junior Camara to race for Haas
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Ferrari protege Rafael Camara will make his Formula 1 debut in 2027 after signing a multi-year deal to race for Haas.

The team was blown away by Camara's performance in his Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) outing with the team at Portimao in August, where he set an impressive pace in Haas's 2025 F1 car.

That helped Camara beat the likes of McLaren reserve driver Leonardo Fornaroli, Toyota's Ryo Hirakawa, and ex-Alpine F1 driver Jack Doohan in the race to replace incumbent Esteban Ocon.

Ocon's two years at Haas have fallen short of expectations as he has generally been outpaced by Ferrari junior Ollie Bearman.

The Race revealed Haas would split with Ocon during the Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend, where it was also known that Camara was the clear favourite to replace him.

Camara won back-to-back titles in the Formula Regional European Championship (an intermediate step between Formula 4 and Formula 3) and F3 in consecutive years before stepping up to Formula 2 in 2026.

The 21-year-old Brazilian currently leads a closely contested F2 championship with two scheduled rounds (Qatar and Abu Dhabi) remaining.

He has won three races and has had a standout qualifying average of 2.54, but it’s been far from a straightforward campaign, with Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu even referencing Camara's tricky weekends - he made a mistake that cost him victory in Monaco and made another costly error in Montreal - in Haas's announcement.

"I'm really excited to sign such a young, amazing talent like Rafael Camara," Komatsu said.

"I don't need to tell everyone about his achievements in the junior formulas, it's been very impressive, and in his rookie season in Formula 2, the speed he's shown in some very difficult moments, like qualifying in Monaco and Montreal - that all goes to show the potential Rafa has.

"He showed when we had him drive in our TPC programme in Portugal that he could handle himself very well [and] with not a huge amount of time to learn the car, he showed us more than just raw speed.

"Rafa managed to create an environment to get the best out of himself, it was very impressive and certainly the laps he completed were special."

Camara has been a member of the Ferrari driver academy since he was in karting in 2021, and will graduate to F1 as its most decorated junior driver ever.

Should Camara win a third consecutive (main season) junior single-seater title, he'll be the first since Oscar Piastri won FREC-F3-F2 in 2019-21.

Camara said he was "very happy" to be joining Haas and thanked Komatsu and Haas F1 team owner Gene Haas for the trust they had placed in him.

"I'm also very grateful to the Scuderia Ferrari driver academy for their support and for everything they have contributed to my development over the years, as well as to my family for always being there throughout this journey," Camara said.

"Now my focus is on preparing myself in the best possible way for this new challenge. There will be a lot to learn, and I'm looking forward to working closely with the team, understanding the car and continuing to develop as a driver."

There is no official confirmation, but Bearman is expected to be retained and form an all-Ferrari-junior line-up alongside Camara.

Komatsu has repeatedly affirmed that those Ferrari links have not influenced Haas's 2026 driver line-up and Camara has been chosen completely on merit.

items.title: What you need to know about F1's new driver - Rafael Camara
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
- Rafael Camara is Formula 1's newest driver as he'll form part of Haas's 2027 driver line-up.

Back in Azerbaijan - where it emerged Camara was highly likely to replace Esteban Ocon - Josh Suttill spoke to Camara and his Invicta F2 team boss James Robinson to find out more about his 2026 season and how he feels being on the brink of F1.

You can read the article below, first published in September 2026.

"I've never met a driver who is so naturally talented as he is."

If you speak to anyone who has worked with likely 2027 Formula 1 driver Rafael Camara, you'll get a similar response to the above.

Humble and softly-spoken out of the car, Camara can be ruthlessly fast inside the cockpit, delivering qualifying laps that blow his rivals out of the water, but with the racecraft of a rough diamond.

The chief characteristic that has fundamentally made Camara an F2 title contender this year and explains why he's impressed Haas enough to consider signing him is that he's .

Just look at the qualifying average from F2 this season and rookie Camara's advantage is clear, with only second-year driver Alex Dunne coming close.

1 Rafael Camara 2.542 Alex Dunne 3.774 Martinius Stenshorne 7.546 Joshua Duerksen 8.388 Dino Beganovic 9.23

9 Tasanapol Inthraphuvasak 10.38

10 Gabriele Mini 10.92 

You have to go back to 2021 F2 champion Oscar Piastri to find a driver pick up so many poles (five) in F2 as a rookie and for a driver with a better average qualifying record.

It was that searing raw speed that was also the bedrock of his 2025 Formula 3 title campaign, too, as he was on pole for four of the first five feature races.

"The speed is just incredible. I've never met a driver who is so naturally talented as he is. He has a feeling for the tyres I've never seen before. It's so natural," Camara's Invicta F2 team boss Robinson told The Race.

"As soon as he stepped in the car, you could see that this guy had something, had a natural speed and feel that we hadn't seen before." 

That's strong praise from an Invicta team that has run Audi F1 driver Gabriel Bortoleto and McLaren reserve (and fellow 2027 Haas F1 seat contender) Leonardo Fornaroli to F2 titles in 2024 and 2025.

Invicta had plenty of drivers offering their services for 2026, but Camara's raw speed had been so impressive even before F3, he'd long been on the team's radar. 

Camara is by no means the finished article. Much like the last Ferrari junior to graduate to F1, Ollie Bearman (ironically Camara's likely 2027 team-mate), alongside the insane raw speed there are still rough edges to his racecraft, by his own admission. 

His speed in F2 has been present since pre-season testing, but his early season was blighted by major errors in Montreal and Monaco.

In Montreal, he spun himself out by diving down the inside of fellow Ferrari junior Dino Beganovic into Turn 2 when the door was already closed.

And then in Monaco, Camara lost a near-certain win by struggling to fire up his tyres on the outlap after his pitstop and then locking up and going down the escape road at Turn 1 while under pressure from title rival Nikola Tsolov. 

"We can be quite happy with what we have done this year, but for sure there were some moments that could be easily avoided," Camara told The Race.

"Some mistakes that I think maybe cost us a bit too much points. There was Montreal that I think was a really stupid move. 

"Then Monaco, in a way, we had everything so under control. This year the outlap was very tricky. By being a bit more on the safe side, I snowballed. Then after it was a big problem.

"We know that Monaco is impossible to overtake, so I didn't want to lose the race. Then I ended up in a much worse place than just being P2. 

"But overall I think it has been a very good season, because I think every time that we had done a mistake, or something that was not the ideal thing or the right thing, we've always been able to learn and to grow. 

"This is how I really see this season, I think I really grew as a driver, also with the team, getting more comfortable with everyone." 

Camara hasn't been able to completely cut out the errors - despite following up that rough early patch with inspired wins at Barcelona and Spa. 

The Madring feature race perfectly summed up the duality of his racecraft, as having pulled off a remarkably bold move on his title rival Tsolov, Camara followed it up by going a step too far with a bolder move that sent Oliver Goethe into the wall and earned Camara a 10-second time penalty.

"He's generally a very calm head in the car and doesn't often make mistakes," Robinson said.

"He has made a couple this year. I think the downfall, if you compare it to, say, Leonardo [Fornaroli, 2025 F2 champion] last season, the big difference between those two years, Leo didn't make any big mistakes at all. That was the recipe for him winning the championship with a round to spare. 

"Rafa has a speed that is undeniable. He's worked hard this year. All he needed to do really was just cut out those silly mistakes that cost him in Montreal and Monaco, for example, and get off the line well. 

"If he can do those things, then he's pretty good at winning races." 

Baku was another example, as after his sprint race was ruined by picking up a 10-second time penalty for locking up and running into the back of Aston Martin junior Mari Boya, Camara rebounded brilliantly on Saturday to win the second feature race and jump back into the points lead. 

Camara's conversations with his Invicta race engineer Pau Rivera, who has engineered the likes of Bortoleto and Zhou Guanyu on their way to F1, have been popular additions to F2's highlight reels this year.

In Montreal, Rivera told Camara: "That's not the way, mate, that's not the way, so now you need to keep it cool and reset" and after Camara lost the Monaco win, he remarkably asked Camara over the radio: "What was the issue on this lap? Why the f*** did you go so slow? We had a massive margin! What the f*** happened there?"

Those conversations drew plenty of attention on social media, but for Camara it's simply evidence of an honest relationship between driver and race engineer. 

"Since the beginning we always had a very nice relationship, we've always been very transparent to each other," Camara explained.

"In the races and the sessions, we're both more excited, and I think sometimes if we don't do the perfect job or if we don't maximise, for sure we're going to be a bit upset.

"Probably in those moments we can discuss a bit more. But it's still nothing really personal. It's just us trying to always maximise and do the best of what we can do together."  

Asked if Camara was ready for F1, Robinson replied: "100%. I'd be very, very surprised if he doesn't race in Formula 1". 

Camara is yet to partake in an F1 practice session, but he has been clocking plenty of laps for both Ferrari and Haas as part of their Testing of Previous Cars programmes - teams are allowed to test pre-2026 cars on up to 20 days this year, with race drivers limited to 1000km total mileage. 

It was Camara's speed he showed Haas, which also tried out Jack Doohan, Fornaroli and reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa, in the TPC tests that has been a huge factor in him becoming the favourite to replace Ocon.

Camara said of his TPC running: "The tests we did with the TPCs have been always positive.

"I was able always to learn and to grow up during these tests…I'm pleased with what I did.

"Also, it was very nice to get this amount of tests [in] F1, so also in a way for us to be more prepared and in a good shape."

So would Camara be ready for F1 if he was given a race seat for 2027?

He replies: "Yes, I don't see why not. I think at the end of the day you're [still] driving fast cars in a circuit [in F1]. So I've been doing this for quite a while.

"It's a very different place. There's a lot more things going on. But I think that it's more really outside of the car.

"In the car, you just do your job and try to always maximise what you can. I think it's the thing that I enjoy the most. It will be always a pleasure to be driving.

"If I'm there it's also a dream, because you're working your whole life for that.

"Obviously it's always nice to get TPCs, but you don't want to just get the taste and not be there the whole time.

"It will be something nice and I think I'm ready."

items.title: The 2027 F1 grid: Every confirmed driver
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
The 2027 grid so far hasn't brought the seismic changes some expected.

Below you'll find the confirmed seats for F1 2027 so far.

Lando NorrisOscar Piastri

Lando Norris signed a new deal keeping him at McLaren until "at least 2030" with options to extend beyond then, while Oscar Piastri has a contract in place that should keep him at the team unti the end of 2028.

George Russell*Kimi Antonelli*

George Russell and Kimi Antonelli were only confirmed for 2026 in October 2025, and nothing beyond 2026 was communicated within that announcement, although The Race understands both drivers have multi-year deals with various options that can be triggered for extensions.

So while not officially confirmed for 2027, there's no reason to believe the line-up will change.

Max VerstappenIsack Hadjar

Back in 2022, Max Verstappen signed a dealto keep him at Red Bull until 2028 and ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix he extended that deal to 2030.

Verstappen's new 2026 team-mate Isack Hadjar received a new deal announced just before his return after a wrist injury, in Baku.

Charles LeclercLewis Hamilton

Charles Leclerc signed a bumper long-term deal in January 2024 for "several more seasons" and signed an extension to that earlier this year, which will keep him at Ferrari well beyond 2027.

Lewis Hamilton will remain for a third year.

Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon committed to racing for Williams in 2027 on the eve of the Dutch GP.

Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad are Racing Bulls' driver pairing for 2026, but neither knows if they'll be continuing into 2027 yet.

Lance StrollFernando Alonso

After much speculation, Fernando Alonso decided to stick around racing in F1 in 2027, alongside Lance Stroll.

Ollie Bearman*Rafael Camara

Nico HulkenbergGabriel Bortoleto

Both Nico Hulkenberg and Gabriel Bortoleto signed for Audi on "multi-year" deals back in 2024. At the Azerbaijan Grand Prix in September 2026, Mattia Binotto said both drivers were contracted at the team for 2027 and that Audi didn't even feel the need to announce the fact. Secure!

Pierre GaslyFranco Colapinto

Midway through 2025, Pierre Gasly's Alpine deal was extended through to the end of 2028.

Franco Colapinto's form was rewarded with a new deal for 2027, just prior to the Italian GP in September 2026.

Sergio PerezValtteri Bottas

Cadillac's first F1 driver line-up of Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas both signed up for the team on "multi-year" deals from 2026.

: Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri: Kimi Antonelli and George Russell*: Isack Hadjar and Max Verstappen: Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc: Alex Albon and Carlos Sainz: TBC: Lance Stroll and Fernando Alonso: Ollie Bearman* and Rafael Camara: Gabriel Bortoleto and Nico Hulkenberg: Franco Colapinto and Pierre Gasly: Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez

*yet to be officially confirmed

items.title: How Red Bull has improved its F1 engine without ADUO
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Lewis Hamilton is calling it the most powerful engine in Formula 1. Toto Wolff says it's clearly not lagging behind. The FIA has officially labelled it the benchmark.

After Max Verstappen’s back-to-back wins in Malaysia and Singapore, the paddock consensus is clear that Red Bull’s recent gains have come as much from the power unit as from its chassis.

Yes, the team's Baku upgrade delivered the downforce step and a more consistent aero platform that has put Verstappen in a super happy place with the balance.

But in F1 2026, cars and drivers are nowhere if the power unit is not up to the job – and on this front Red Bull Power Trains (RBPT) is no longer playing clear second fiddle to championship leaders Mercedes.

Telemetry traces and those ghost lap replays have highlighted that Red Bull’s poles have been won as much on the straights as the corners – with a top speed profile that was not there earlier in the year.

As Hamilton said after being unable to challenge Verstappen in the Singapore sprint: “To overtake the most powerful engine on the grid is not so easy.”

What is fascinating about this shift in the battle between power unit manufacturers – where once Mercedes was a step above everyone – is that it has happened without any hardware steps.

While Ferrari has used both of the upgrades it is allowed under the ADUO (Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities) rules, neither Mercedes nor Red Bull has brought any new homologations.

Mercedes is holding fire until at least the United States Grand Prix, while Red Bull can't have anything new because it's been ruled as the benchmark engine (twice) by the FIA’s analysis.

But just because there have been no specification updates doesn't mean Red Bull hasn't unlocked more performance.

The story of its season, and how it's at a point where rivals are admiring what it's doing, is because it's more consistently using the full potential of its power unit.

Like a car's peaky aero package that delivers a lot of downforce in a very narrow window, Red Bull's power unit shone - but not at every track and every lap.

But there was no evidence of that characteristic being there regularly over the first half of the season. Mercedes looked to be in a class of its own.

Looking at how things have changed, RBPT’s technical director Ben Hodgkinson told us the key steps forward are coming from calibration work – which has involved fuel supplier Exxon Mobil and Red Bull's own engineers at Milton Keynes.

This is effectively detailed work to marry up power output, fuel consumption, energy harvesting, and deployment strategies.

“We've sort of found that the most powerful engine that we can create has made a combustion system that is quite challenging to make sure you always get the maximum performance out of it,” Hodgkinson told The Race,

“That's put an awful lot of pressure onto the calibration team to try and make sure that it's always working at that right level.”

The picture at the start of the season of how things looked between Mercedes and Red Bull was also exacerbated by decisions taken at Milton Keynes to hold fire in committing to its design.

It elected to keep developing longer than originally planned. This meant it was still pushing forward with its design when, ideally, it should have been doing the preparation work on durability and calibration.

“At our original point in the pre-season, when we were planning to freeze the spec, we weren't really happy with the performance levels,” said Hodgkinson.

“So we made the decision to just keep going, which was giving us less and less time to do durability runs and do all the calibration work that we needed to do.

“We actually started the season with quite immature calibrations. But they have got better and better throughout every single race.”

Hodgkinson says the improvements have never stopped and there was a “nice step of learning” between the Baku weekend and Sepang – where that maiden RBPT win was delivered.

“This was able to make sure that the engine was performing closer to its best at all times,” he said.

“We sort of have an engine that sometimes underperforms to what we know it can do. There has always been this prize that if you can get it performing at the top of its range for every single lap, we're going to be in a really good place.”

But it's not just understanding the power unit in isolation that Red Bull has made progress this year. The F1 2026 rules have meant power units and chassis are having to work in closer unison than ever before, and this is an area where things have moved a lot at Milton Keynes.

Hodgkinson adds, “There's been a much, much deeper collaboration between the chassis and the PU side.

“It is about how you balance energy and deploy it, where you can harvest it and working with the drivers. I can really see how that team is just getting stronger and stronger. When we win, it really is a one-team victory - evidence of us all coming together.”

Verstappen’s back-to-back wins in Malaysia and Singapore, plus the pace it showed in Baku, have shown that the Red Bull package is not lacking anywhere.

As Wolff said: “You can’t see that it’s lagging. They have done it very well. The ICE seems to be very competitive. Obviously, you can see that with ADUO, but also in terms of energy recovery and energy deployment there. It’s pretty good.”

Hodgkinson thinks the RBPT is not at its peak yet – with the ever-improving calibration pointing to further gains this year.

“There's still improvement to be had just from the calibration side, so I think that you'll see a bit of that this season,” he said.

And then of course it must not be forgotten that a new fuel flow regime and a change of turbo boost pressure will somewhat reset the power units in 2027.

“What should have been a year of refining things is kind of a year of going again on the combustion system,” said Hodgkison, who sees opportunity for gains even if RBPT remains without any extra ADUO allowances.

“We've learned an awful lot about how to get the best out of this combustion system, and so the changes that we're making for next season are from that learning.”

Hodgkinson is not the sort of person who is happy to rest on his laurels.

“I think there's a lot that could still be got through the calibration,” he said. “I can see our engine; there's still a margin to its theoretical best that we see on dynos.

“And actually, it's not all down to calibration to solve that. You can make some hardware changes that make it a bit easier too, or a bit less of a diva, to try and use some terminology that's often used in F1.

“Our combustion system could be described as a bit of a diva, and we need to make it slightly easier to extract the best out of it.

“So that's some of the changes that we're making for next year, and hopefully we can get a nice step on in performance.”

It is little wonder Mercedes is predicting a tougher title battle than it's had this year.

Wolff said after Singapore: "One thing is for sure: next year it's full-on the fight between the teams and Red Bull is part of that."

items.title: Red Bull's F1 boss gets well-timed endorsement with extended deal
items.author: Matt Beer
items.content:
Red Bull has given a very strong endorsement of Laurent Mekies' leadership by publicly announcing the extension of his contract as its Formula 1 team principal through 2031.

Though it is increasingly common for F1 team principals both to be on specific-term contracts rather than rolling employee deals, and for extensions of those deals to be announced in public, Red Bull's strong display of faith in Mekies still stands out as a message the company hierarchy clearly wanted the world to hear.

He was swiftly moved across from junior team Racing Bulls when Christian Horner was ousted from Red Bull last summer.

The Red Bull press release announcing Mekies’ new deal specifically highlighted that "under Laurent’s leadership, the team delivered a remarkable turnaround during the second half of the 2025 season, ultimately missing out on the drivers’ championship by just two points".

The announcement of Mekies’ new deal comes after Max Verstappen’s decision to commit to Red Bull for the long term, the team extending Isack Hadjar’s deal, and Verstappen taking back to back wins in Malaysia and Singapore.

It also coincides with Mekies’ predecessor Horner being back in the public eye around the launch of his new book and an associated run of interviews in which his time at - and exit from - Red Bull are a major topic.

A joint comment from Red Bull shareholders Chalerm Yoovidhya and Mark Mateschitz read: "Laurent has played a crucial role in guiding the team through an important period of transition while maintaining the competitive spirit and the Red Bull principles that define us.

"This extension reflects our confidence in his leadership and our shared belief in the long-term vision of the team."
